H1.text: A sponge. A jellyfish. A cockroach.

H2.text: One has no organs. One has no head. One has six jointed legs. Yet all three are animals.

H3.text: Diya found all three on one page of her zoology book, and asked: how do biologists sort animals this different?

H4.text: Over a million species of animals have been described.

H5.text: By the end, you will know the six body features used to sort every animal.

B1.text: So how do you sort a million animals?

B2.text: Not by looks. A bat and a crow both fly, but the bat is a mammal and the crow is a bird.

B3.text: Biologists look at the body plan instead: how the body is built, from cells to layers and cavities.

B4.text: Shared features become the bases of classification. A basis is simply a feature we sort by.

Z1.text: Look closely at the three animals on Diya's page.

Z2.text: The sponge is a hollow body with tiny pores, the ostia. Water flows in through them.

Z3.text: Inside is a cavity, the spongocoel. Water leaves through the big opening on top, the osculum.

Z4.text: The jellyfish has a soft bell with tentacles at its edge. Cut it through the centre in any direction, and the halves match.

Z5.text: The cockroach has a head, a thorax and an abdomen, with jointed legs and long antennae.

Z6.text: Very different bodies. So biologists ask every animal the same six questions.

L2.text: One. Level of organisation. Do the cells work loosely, or form tissues, organs and organ systems?

L3.text: Two. Symmetry. Does a cut give two matching halves, and in how many directions?

L4.text: Three. Germ layers. Does the embryo, the animal at its earliest stage, build two layers or three?

L5.text: Four. Coelom. Is there a body cavity between the gut and the body wall, lined by mesoderm, the middle germ layer?

L6.text: Five. Segmentation. Is the body built from repeated segments, like an earthworm?

L7.text: Six. Notochord. Does the embryo form a stiff rod along its back? It splits chordates from non-chordates.

L8.text: Biologists also compare systems. Is the gut a bag with one opening, or a tube with two?

T1.text: Remember this. Animals are sorted by their body plan, not by their looks.

C1.text: Now run all three animals through the questions.

C2.text: One. The sponge's cells work loosely, with no true tissues: the cellular level. The jellyfish has tissues. The cockroach has organ systems.

C3.text: Two. The sponge has no symmetry. The jellyfish is radial: many cuts work. The cockroach is bilateral: only one cut gives matching halves.

C4.text: Three. The jellyfish builds two germ layers: diploblastic. The cockroach builds three: triploblastic.

C5.text: Four. The cockroach has a coelom. The sponge and the jellyfish have no body cavity.

C6.text: Five. The cockroach is segmented. The other two are not.

C7.text: Six. None of them forms a notochord. All three are non-chordates.

U1.text: But careful. One feature alone can fool you.

U2.text: A jellyfish is radial. It has two germ layers and no body cavity.

U3.text: A starfish is radial too, but it has three germ layers and a true coelom, and its larva is bilateral.

U4.text: Your turn. A jellyfish and a starfish are both radial. Are they in the same phylum? Pause and decide.

U5.text: No! The starfish is an echinoderm, the jellyfish a coelenterate. The symmetry matched, but the germ layers and the coelom did not.

P1.text: Put the answers together, and they make one branching map.

P2.text: Cells only, with no tissues: the sponges, phylum Porifera.

P3.text: Two germ layers: the coelenterates and the comb jellies.

P4.text: Three germ layers, and then the cavity decides: none in flatworms, a false one in roundworms, a true coelom in the rest.

P5.text: Last, the notochord splits the true-coelom animals into non-chordates and chordates.

W1.text: Now, a worked example: an earthworm after the rain.

W2.text: Level: its organs form organ systems.

W3.text: Symmetry: only one cut, down the middle, gives matching halves. Bilateral.

W5.text: Coelom: yes, a true coelom. Segments: yes, a chain of rings.

W6.text: No notochord. So the earthworm is a non-chordate, in phylum Annelida.

X2.text: Many students think a sponge is a plant, because it stays fixed in one place.

X3.text: But a sponge has no cell walls and no chlorophyll, and it takes its food from the water flowing through it. It is an animal.

E1.text: Where is this asked? As statement or match questions on a group's level, symmetry, germ layers or coelom.

Q1.text: Exam level now. Match each feature with the right animal group. Pause and solve.

A2.text: Sponges are at the cellular level. Coelenterates are diploblastic.

A3.text: Flatworms have no body cavity, so they are acoelomates. And the earthworm shows metameric segmentation.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Name the six features used to classify animals.

Y3.text: Two. Why is symmetry alone not enough to place an animal?

Y4.text: Three. Is a sponge a plant or an animal, and why?

N1.text: Next time: a crowd, a team and a machine. Do cells work alone, or as a team? We find out in levels of organisation.
